english: But Plato and those of his school acknowledge indeed that God is uncreated, and the Father and Maker of all things; but then they maintain that matter as well as God is uncreated, and aver that it is coeval with God.
translator: Marcus Dods (ANF vol. 2 text; ANC 1867 vol. 3 scan)
page: ANF vol. 2 printed p. 194 (PDF p. 215 footer)
edition: The Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 2 (Roberts & Donaldson, ed.; Buffalo 1885), CCEL PDF cache, 1368 pp.
what_it_says: Theophilus rejects uncreated matter coeval with God; only God is uncreated, so God alone made all things.
limits: Context for 2.10 (creation from nothing). Says nothing about Word or Spirit directly.

english: God, then, having His own Word internal within His own bowels, begat Him, emitting Him along with His own wisdom before all things. He had this Word as a helper in the things that were created by Him, and by Him He made all things. He is called "governing principle" [harke], because He rules, and is Lord of all things fashioned by Him. He, then, being Spirit of God, and governing principle, and wisdom, and power of the highest, came down upon the prophets
translator: Marcus Dods (ANF vol. 2 text; ANC 1867 vol. 3 scan)
page: ANF vol. 2 printed p. 204 (PDF p. 225 footer)
edition: The Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 2 (Roberts & Donaldson, ed.; Buffalo 1885), CCEL PDF cache, 1368 pp.
what_it_says: God begat His internal Word, emitting Him with His wisdom before all things; this Word is the agent of creation and is also called "Spirit of God" and "wisdom" in the same clause.
limits: This is the hard passage: the Word is "begat" and "emitted" at a point before creation (the endiathetos/prophorikos language is not checked in Greek). It also equates Word, Spirit of God and wisdom in one clause. Defenders (Bull, Newman, Kelly) argue the begetting is eternal and the language is pre-Nicene; no "homoousios". The Greek is not checked.

english: In like manner also the three days which were before the luminaries, are types of the Trinity, of God, and His Word, and His wisdom. And the fourth is the type of man, who needs light, that so there may be God, the Word, wisdom, man.
translator: Marcus Dods (ANF vol. 2 text; ANC 1867 vol. 3 scan)
page: ANF vol. 2 printed p. 212 (PDF p. 233 footer); footnote 64 on the same page
edition: The Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 2 (Roberts & Donaldson, ed.; Buffalo 1885), CCEL PDF cache, 1368 pp.
what_it_says: Theophilus calls the three days before the luminaries "types of the Trinity", naming God, His Word and His wisdom.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (word Triad/Trinity) and objection
limits: The triad is God, Word, Wisdom, with no Holy Spirit named; the "first use of Trinity" claim is the ANF editors' footnote (fn. 64, which gives "Τριάδος" in Greek and says "the earliest use of this word"), not Theophilus. Greek not checked.

english: For God having made all things by His Word, and having reckoned them all mere bye-works, reckons the creation of man to be the only work worthy of His own hands. ... But to no one else than to His own Word and wisdom did He say, "Let Us make."
translator: Marcus Dods (ANF vol. 2 text; ANC 1867 vol. 3 scan)
page: ANF vol. 2 printed p. 215 (PDF p. 236 footer)
edition: The Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 2 (Roberts & Donaldson, ed.; Buffalo 1885), CCEL PDF cache, 1368 pp.
what_it_says: God addresses "Let Us make" (Gen. 1:26) only to His own Word and wisdom, who act with Him.
limits: Word and wisdom are the co-addressees of the plural; the Spirit is absent here. Arian readers take the Word as a subordinate agent. Ellipsis omits the middle sentence. Greek not checked.

english: But what else is this voice but the Word of God, who is also His Son? Not as the poets and writers of myths talk of the sons of gods begotten from intercourse [with women], but as truth expounds, the Word, that always exists, residing within the heart of God. For before anything came into being He had Him as a counsellor, being His own mind and thought. But when God wished to make all that He determined on, He begot this Word, uttered, the first-born of all creation, not Himself being emptied of the Word [Reason], but having begotten Reason, and always conversing with His Reason.
translator: Marcus Dods (ANF vol. 2 text; ANC 1867 vol. 3 scan)
page: ANF vol. 2 printed p. 219 (PDF p. 240 footer)
edition: The Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 2 (Roberts & Donaldson, ed.; Buffalo 1885), CCEL PDF cache, 1368 pp.
what_it_says: The Word is "also His Son", was "counsellor" with God before creation, and was "begot" and "uttered" as first-born of creation.
use: objection (Son is rare) and answer to objection (eternal Word, no emptying)
limits: This is the only place in the Books read here where "Son" is used with the Word (note: "Son" occurs rarely per the brief). "Begot ... uttered" is the same hard language as 2.10. Greek not checked; bracketed words are Dods's.
